title: My GrandOrgue Implementation
text:
Executive Summary
This site documents my experience setting up, configuring, and using a GrandOrgue virtual pipe organ (VPO). As of 2026, there was little compiled documentation other than how to download the software. Information such as system and hardware requirements was scattered throughout the internet, but one generally had to find it through a search engine. Some of this information was later discovered within the GrandOrgue Help pages, but that was after downloading, installing, and digging into the software. I wanted to know what I needed before starting the project to determine whether it was feasible. For example, could I use a Raspberry Pi or would I need something more powerful? Lots of community user experiences were captured in hundreds of issues and thousands of discussions on the official GitHub repo. It all felt very scattered. This site attempts to organize my research, trials, and errors.
These pages are my contribution to the open source GrandOrgue project and its outstanding user community. I hope these pages help you build and enjoy your own GrandOrgue virtual pipe organ.

title: Hardware Requirements
text:
Discussion
GrandOrgue is free open source computer software supported for Windows, MacOS, and at least some Linux distributions. System and hardware requirements are summarized here, with the most important requirement being RAM.
My initial installation was intended to be a proof-of-concept learning experiment to assess whether or not it was something I wanted to delve further into and scale up. I already had an old (circa 1997) Casio MIDI keyboard1, so I decided to use that as the workbench test case for experimentation. Then, once I knew what I was doing and felt comfortable with the technical components, I wanted to transfer the setup to a MIDI-ready digital church organ to try it out “in the field” with an actual organ console, decent speakers, and a room where an organ is regularly used.
With this in mind, I sought portability with minimal spatial footprint. Desktop computers took up too much space and are not easily portable, so they were out. Without having a personal organ at home, I needed to interface with the software directly through the computer rather than via an organ console, so I wanted to have a touch screen monitor that could be positioned in close proximity to the music keyboard. While standard laptops with touch screens are portable and could work, I would have to always reach over the laptop keyboard to reach the screen, which was not ideal. My solution was to use a Raspberry Pi together with a simple touch screen monitor.
I opted for the Raspberry Pi 5 because it was the first and, as of 2026, only unit to contain 16 GB of RAM. I purchased a full CanaKit starter kit which included:

Raspberry Pi 5 with 2.4Ghz 64-bit quad-core CPU and 64 GB of RAM
128GB Micro SD Card pre-loaded with 64-bit Raspberry Pi OS, USB MicroSD Card Reader
Plastic protective case
Low noise bearing system fan
Heat sink
45W PD Power Supply
2 6-foot display cables

I bought a simple and compact 15.6” portable touch screen monitor for my primary means of interacting with GrandOrgue. An upgrade might be in store down the road, but this will due to start.
Unfortunately, the Raspberry Pi 5 does not have a dedicated 3.5mm headphone audio jack like its predecessor. Audio is outputted through HDMI or USB instead. I ended up buying a Behringer UMC204HD USB audio interface which would allow me to use a single USB port for both audio and to connect standard MIDI cables instead of a MIDI-USB cable. I also bought a 9.8-foot dual 5-pin MIDI cable to go along with that because I did not have one already.
Altogether, my expenses for the initial set up came out to be just over $600:

Total cost of my initial proof-of-concept setup.

title: Digital Organ
text:
This page describes how to set up GrandOrgue with a MIDI-equipped digital organ.

Connect the touchscreen monitor to the Raspberry Pi (RPi) using an HDMI cable and a USB cable plugged into a white USB 2.0 port. The monitor needs both cables to handle video, audio, and mouse commands.
Connect the Behringer UMC204HD USB audio interface to the RPi using a USB cable plugged into a blue USB 3.0 port.
Connect the organ MIDI OUT to the audio interface MIDI IN. This enables the organ console to control the GrandOrgue software. Since the software won’t be controlling the organ console in any way, there is no need for a second MIDI cable. If the organ has separate switched and unswitched MIDI ports, using switched ports will require the divisional MIDI stops to be engaged in order for the virtual organ to sound through the speakers, while using unswitched ports will allow the virtual organ to speak regardless of whether the divisional MIDI stops are engaged. The second option is more intuitive for most applications.
To utilize the digital organ speakers, connect the audio interface AUDIO OUT to audio line inputs on the organ. This will require either two 1/4” TRS or a two-channel RCA cable, depending on the organ.
If using an external keyboard or mouse, connect to it to the RPi using either the white USB 2.0 port (preferred) or the remaining blue USB 3.0 port.
Connect the power supplies to the RPi.

title: Software
text:
Raspberry Pi setup
Raspberry Pi (RPi) devices run Debian-based Raspberry Pi OS. GrandOrgue needs the 64-bit Raspberry Pi OS in order to utilize all of the installed RAM (a 32-bit OS would cap the usable RAM at 4 GB, regardless of what is installed in the system.) The 64-bit OS conveniently comes pre-installed on the CanaKit RPi.
Before installing anything, download and install any OS updates:
GrandOrgue recommends X11 to properly handle window sizing and positioning. To switch the display mode:
The touch monitor is plug-and-play. Since the RPi 5 only has a single USB-C port, which is used for the power supply, the monitor needs to be connected to the RPi via both HDMI for data and USB for power. I used the HDMI to mini-HDMI cable that came with the RPi and the USB-C to USB-A cable that came with the monitor. The RPi needed to be rebooted after everything was connected for the touch screen to work properly.

title: Software
text:
sudo apt update && sudo apt full-upgrade -y
sudo reboot


Open a terminal and run
sudo raspi-config
Use the down arrow key to select Advanced Options
In the next menu, select Wayland
Select X11, then <OK>
Use the right arrow key to select <Finish> and then Reboot



Set Screen Resolution
The Pi occasionally fails to read the monitor’s EDID (Extended Display Identification Data) on boot and defaults to 1024x768. Force the correct resolution by adding these lines to the boot config:
sudo nano /boot/firmware/config.txt
Add at the bottom:
hdmi_force_hotplug=1
hdmi_group=2
hdmi_mode=82
hdmi_force_hotplug=1 — forces Pi to treat HDMI as always connected
hdmi_group=2 — sets DMT (Display Monitor Timings) mode for computer monitors
hdmi_mode=82 — forces 1920x1080 at 60Hz


Touch screen right-click
There was no discernable way to right-click on the touch screen by default on the X11 release of Raspberry Pi OS. This can be fixed by telling X11, the software layer that manages the display and interprets input, to treat a specific pattern of touch behavior, such as briefly holding a finger still on a spot, as a right-click signal. To do this, we need to set three settings:

EmulateThirdButton to turns the feature on
EmulateThirdButtonTimeout to set how long to hold before it triggers, in milliseconds. 750 is long enough that normal taps don’t accidentally trigger it, but short enough to feel responsive.
EmulateThirdButtonMoveThreshold to set how many pixels your finger is allowed to drift during the hold before the gesture is cancelled. This prevents accidental right-clicks when you’re just resting your finger briefly while scrolling or moving around the screen.

Open a terminal window and enter:
sudo nano /usr/share/X11/xorg.conf.d/99-ilitek-touch.conf
If this file exists, add the following inside the Section "InputClass" block:
Option "EmulateThirdButton" "1"
Option "EmulateThirdButtonTimeout" "750"
Option "EmulateThirdButtonMoveThreshold" "30"
If the file that opens is blank, paste the following in it:
Section "InputClass"
    Identifier "ILITEK Touch"
    MatchProduct "ILITEK ILITEK-TP"
    MatchIsTouchscreen "on"
    Option "TransformationMatrix" "1 0 0 0 1 0 0 0 1"
    Option "EmulateThirdButton" "1"
    Option "EmulateThirdButtonTimeout" "750"
    Option "EmulateThirdButtonMoveThreshold" "30"
EndSection
This does two things: maps the touch device correctly to the display and enables long-press (750ms hold) as right-click emulation. Save the file and reboot the machine. Touch screen right-clicking should now be supported.


On screen keyboard
The X11 release of Raspberry Pi OS also does not natively support an on-screen touch keyboard. To avoid needing an external keyboard, install and configure onboard, a decent on-screen keyboard for X11 on Raspberry Pi:
sudo apt install onboard
To make this keyboard automatically appear when needed, like on a tablet or smartphone, also install AT-SPI2, the Linux Assistive Technology Service Provider Interface, and enable accessibility:
sudo apt install at-spi2-core
gsettings set org.gnome.desktop.interface toolkit-accessibility true
Configure the keyboard to your liking using its built-in settings:
onboard-settings
I chose to dock it to the bottom of the screen and stretch across the screen, like on a tablet:

Window → enable “Dock to screen edge”
Window → Docking Settings → select “Shrink workarea”, “Expand on landscape screens”, and “Expand on portrait screens”
Window → Docking Settings → select “Dock to screen edge: Bottom”

And to auto-show when needed:

Auto-show → “Auto-show when editing text”

This does not behave as flawlessly or as conveniently as one is accustomed to on mobile devices, but it is close enough for a system that will primarily be used as a virtual organ. For example, one caveat is that the keyboard application has to be running in order for auto-show to work. Also, the keyboard itself is known to work fine in some applications, not at all in some, and be hit-or-miss in others. To handle this, add a toggle button to the taskbar that can be used to launch the keyboard when first needed or to manually show it if it does not automatically show in some application. This requires three steps:

Create a system-wide .desktop file:
sudo nano /usr/share/applications/onboard.desktop
In it, add the following:
[Desktop Entry]
Name=On-Screen Keyboard
Comment=Toggle On-Screen Keyboard
Exec=bash -c 'DISPLAY=:0 killall onboard || DISPLAY=:0 onboard'
Icon=onboard
Type=Application
Categories=Utility;
Modify the system panel file to add it to the taskbar:
nano ~/.config/lxpanel/LXDE-pi/panels/panel
Add the following block to the end of the file:
Plugin {
  type=launchtaskbar
  Config {
    Button {
      id=onboard.desktop
    }
  }
expand=0
}
Open the keyboard application on startup:
nano ~/.config/lxsession/LXDE-pi/autostart
Add to the end of the file:
@onboard

After these steps, reboot the machine for the settings to take affect.

title: Software
text:
GrandOrgue

Installation
From the GrandOrgue releases GitHub, download the arm64.deb architecture package. As of May 2026, the current release was grandorgue_3.17.1-1_arm64.deb. It can also be downloaded directly in the terminal:
wget https://github.com/GrandOrgue/grandorgue/releases/download/3.17.1-1/grandorgue_3.17.1-1_arm64.deb






Note



grandorgue requires wxWidgets 3.2 and grandorgue-wx30 requires wxWidgets 3.0. Raspberry Pi OS Bookworm ships with wxWidgets 3.2, so the standard grandorgue package above is the correct one.


Install the software using either the downloaded installer or terminal:
sudo apt install ./grandorgue_3.17.1-1_arm64.deb
sudo apt --fix-broken install
You might get a Permission Denied warning, but it can be ignored:
N: Download is performed unsandboxed as root as file '/home/username/grandorgue_3.17.1-1_arm64.deb' couldn't be accessed by user '_apt'. - pkgAcquire::Run (13: Permission denied)
It is not a fatal error; the application should have installed fine.
Verify the installation by looking for it in the Sound & Video application menu. Launch the program. It should open and load the demo organ.


Configuration
Next, we need to map MIDI channels between GrandOrgue and the instrument. Open GrandOrgue and go to File → Settings

MIDI Devices tab: Select UNC204HD as both the MIDI input device and MIDI output device.
Audio tab:

Set Sample Rate to 48000 and Samples per buffer to 128
Under Sound ports, select RtAudio and RtAudio alsa
In the Mapping output panel, under Audio Output, set the Device to RtAudio: alsa: Default ALSA Device [50 ms requested] to route the audio through the built in monitor speakers for now. (To set this, click the name of the current device, then click Change.) See Audio for instructions on changing this later.


To reduce audio lag:

File → Settings → Audio
Set the Samples per buffer to 256 or 128 (defaults to 512).

The lower the buffer size, the lower the latency. At 48,000 Hz sample rate, 128 samples per buffer supposedly gives about 2.7 milliseconds of latency, which is completely imperceptible. The tradeoff is that very low buffer sizes can cause audio crackle or dropouts if the RPi can’t process audio fast enough. The Pi 5 should, however, be plenty powerful enough to handle 128 samples without trouble, especially with the demo sample set.
Even at 128 samples/buffer, I still noticed a lag, but it was better than when I started. It is possible that some delay is “built in” as the result of the sample recording. This remains to be determined. I am accustomed to old-technology, non-realistic digital organs on which the sound is instantaneous, whereas many pipe organs have a slight (fraction of a second) lag between the time a key is depressed and the sound is actually heard.
The overall volume can be controlled via the GrandOrgue menu bar using the + and - buttons next to the small speaker icon. Raise the volume cautiously, watching the audio bars as you play. Going to loud will cause the audio to clip (max out), leading to distortion.


Updating
As of late 2026, GrandOrgue does not include a built-in software update method. While it does display an alert in the menu bar when an update is available, one must manually download and install it. The process is the same as the initial installation:
wget https://github.com/GrandOrgue/grandorgue/releases/download/X.X.X-X/grandorgue_X.X.X-X_arm64.deb
sudo apt install ./grandorgue_X.X.X-X_arm64.deb
sudo apt --fix-broken install
where X.X.X-X is the version release to download. Since I do not use Linux enough to remember these commands, nor can I ever remember the correct asset, I created a simple Shell script to handle it for me:


update_grandorgue.sh

#!/bin/bash
# update-grandorgue.sh
# Downloads and installs a GrandOrgue release from GitHub
# Usage: ./update-grandorgue.sh <version>
# Example: ./update-grandorgue.sh 3.17.3-1

set -e  # Exit immediately if any command fails

# --- Check argument ---
if [ -z "$1" ]; then
    echo "Usage: $0 <version>"
    echo "Example: $0 3.17.3-1"
    echo ""
    echo "Find the latest version at:"
    echo "https://github.com/GrandOrgue/grandorgue/releases"
    exit 1
fi

VERSION="$1"
ARCH="arm64"
FILENAME="grandorgue_${VERSION}_${ARCH}.deb"
URL="https://github.com/GrandOrgue/grandorgue/releases/download/${VERSION}/${FILENAME}"
DOWNLOAD_DIR="/tmp"
DOWNLOAD_PATH="${DOWNLOAD_DIR}/${FILENAME}"

echo "============================================"
echo " GrandOrgue Updater"
echo "============================================"
echo " Version : $VERSION"
echo " File    : $FILENAME"
echo " URL     : $URL"
echo "============================================"
echo ""

# --- Download ---
echo "Downloading $FILENAME..."
wget -O "$DOWNLOAD_PATH" "$URL"

if [ ! -f "$DOWNLOAD_PATH" ]; then
    echo "Error: Download failed. Check the version number and try again."
    exit 1
fi

echo "Download complete."
echo ""

# --- Install ---
echo "Installing $FILENAME..."
sudo apt install -y "$DOWNLOAD_PATH"

echo ""
echo "============================================"
echo " GrandOrgue $VERSION installed successfully."
echo "============================================"

# --- Clean up ---
echo "Cleaning up downloaded file..."
rm "$DOWNLOAD_PATH"
echo "Done."

For convenience, and until I remember that it exists, I put this script on my Desktop alongside GrandOrgue. To use it, open a terminal window, navigate to the Desktop, and launch the code, passing the desired release version as a command line argument:
./update_grandorgue.sh 3.17.3-1


Audio
Several audio routing options exist, but GrandOrgue needs to be configured properly for each one to work. High-quality headphones or external speakers are highly recommended.
To use the touchscreen built-in speakers or headphones or external speakers plugged into the touchscreen headphone jack:

In the Mapping output panel, under Audio Output, set the Device to RtAudio: alsa: Default ALSA Device [50 ms requested]. (To set this, click the name of the current device, then click Change.)

To use headphones or external speakers connected to the USB audio interface (preferred method):

In the Mapping output panel, under Audio Output, set the Device to RtAudio: alsa: UMC204HD 192k (USB Audio) [50 ms requested].
Turn the MIX knob fully clockwise to PS (playback signal) to hear only the audio playback from GrandOrgue. (If set counterclockwise to IN, you won’t hear anything.)
Adjust the volume using the PHONES volume knob.
Toggle the MONITOR button until you hear sound. In my case, it has to be out.

Use the first configuration (RtAudio: alsa: Default ALSA Device [50 ms requested]) for Bluetooth headphone as well, since the audio will be handled by the operating system rather than GrandOrgue. My experience, however, has been that bluetooth headphones experience a fairly significant lag in audio, so I use wired headphones.
Since my old keyboard did not have an Audio In jack, I could not channel the sound back to the keyboard speakers – which was just as well, because they are not very good anyway. The best (but not perfect) option was wired headphones plugged into the UNC204HD interface. The only headphones I owned had a 1/8” plug, so I had to use a 1/4”-1/8” adapter to connect them. There was a slight buzz, possibly resulting from the extra connection. It was annoying, but not bad enough to abandon the setup.

title: Customization
text:
Bureå Funeral Chapel
The default sample set is great to get started with, but it’s rather small. The beauty of virtual pipe organ (VPO) software is the ability and flexibility to use any number of sample sets. Many sample sets of various sizes exist, from small single-division organs to large many-division instruments. One constraint is disk storage: one needs to have enough space to download and store the sample set. The primary constraint with choosing samples to use, however, is RAM: the sample set must fit in the computer’s RAM to work properly. Thus, my constraint was 16 GB RAM that came on the Raspberry Pi 5. What this means in practice:
Since I only had one keyboard with no pedalboard, it made sense to consider single-manual samples. I could use larger ones, but I could only play one manual. The workaround would be mapping the Great division to my keyboard and relying on couplers to play other manuals from the Great manual. (I might also be able to map all manuals to the same keyboard and essentially multiply the number of stops available, but I haven’t tested this yet.)
The first organ I tried was the Bureå Funeral Chapel from Lars Virtual Pipe Organs. This is a small chamber organ with one manual, pedals, and nine stops. All of the manual stops are split stops with separate drawknobs for bass (first two octaves) and everything else. Split stops provide greater flexibility on a small instrument, allowing the organist to use different combinations of stops on one manual instead of across two manuals. Since I only have one keyboard, this seemed like a good starting point.
First, download the .rar file. I needed to install the “unrar” utility the first time in order to extract this:
Next, unpacked it into the GrandOrgue/Organs/ directory:
Finally, open GrandOrgue, go to File → Open, find and select the desired organ sample, and click Open. The new organ should load and be ready for use.

title: Customization
text:
sudo apt install unrar

unrar x Burea_Funeral_Chapel.rar /home/username/GrandOrgue/Organs/Burea_Funeral_Chapel/
